9219.title: Lean Production
9219.heading: Lean Production
9219.content:
Lean production improves the complete stream by which game content moves from need to playable integration. It reduces waste, batch size, queues, and handoffs while using measured cycle time to expose constraints.

The objective is reliable delivery of valuable assets, not maximum utilization of every specialist. Small batches bring production, gameplay, and quality evidence back before large volumes are committed.

9222.title: Lean Development
9222.heading: Lean Development
9222.content:
Lean development improves the whole stream by delivering quickly, reducing waste, building quality into the work, and using the knowledge of the people doing it. Local efficiency is secondary to the movement of value through the complete system.

Its practices include [[Continuous Improvement]], smaller [[Batch Size|batches]], shorter [[Cycle Time|cycle times]], and exposing constraints instead of hiding them with excess inventory or parallel work.

9231.content:
A lazy-loaded route defers downloading and evaluating a route's component bundle until navigation requires it. This reduces the initial JavaScript needed to start the application.

React can load the component through a dynamic import and display fallback content while the code arrives. The boundary is most useful for pages that are substantial or not needed by every user.

9234.title: LDLT Factorization
9234.heading: LDLT Factorization
9234.content:
An LDLT factorization writes a symmetric matrix as $A=LDL^T$, where $L$ is unit lower triangular and $D$ is diagonal.

It separates diagonal scaling from triangular structure and avoids square roots required by [[Cholesky Decomposition]]. The form is useful when symmetry is available even when the matrix is not positive definite.

9237.title: Leading Coefficient
9237.heading: Leading Coefficient
9237.content:
The leading coefficient of a nonzero polynomial is the coefficient of its highest term under the selected ordering. In one variable, this is the coefficient attached to the term whose exponent equals the [[Polynomial Degree]].

In several variables, the leading coefficient depends on a [[Monomial Order]]. Together with the leading monomial it determines the leading term used to build an [[Initial Ideal]] and a [[Gröbner Basis]].

9240.title: Lead Time
9240.heading: Lead Time
9240.content:
Lead time is the elapsed time from identifying a desired feature until it is deployed. Unlike [[Cycle Time]], it includes time the item spends waiting in a backlog before active work begins.

For a live game, lead time measures responsiveness to players and the market. Reducing queues, batch size, low-value backlog inventory, and deployment delay can matter as much as faster development.

9243.content: A layered time-plot annotation adds explanatory marks behind or above the primary [[Time Plot]] without replacing the observed series. Background blocks can distinguish years, translucent regions can flag threshold conditions, and lines or labels can mark averages and extrema. Layer order matters: broad contextual regions should generally be drawn first so they do not hide the data. [[Time-Series Panel Function|Panel functions]] provide one way to control that order.

9246.sourceSearchName: layer wise autoencoder pretraining layer wise autoencoder pretraining
9246.title: Layer-Wise Autoencoder Pretraining
9246.heading: Layer-Wise Autoencoder Pretraining
9246.content:
Greedy layer-wise pretraining trains one [[Autoencoder|encoder]] on raw inputs, keeps its encoding layer, and then trains another encoder to reconstruct that first layer's representation. Repeating this builds a stack of representations before the final prediction task is fitted.

Each layer is optimized for its own reconstruction task rather than the eventual output, which is why the process is called greedy. A later tuning phase can freeze the pretrained layers or adjust the whole network using target labels. Kelleher presents this as an important historical route to useful initial weights for deep networks, while noting that most later deep networks are trained without it.

9249.sourceSearchName: layer matrix computation layer matrix computation
9249.title: Layer Matrix Computation
9249.heading: Layer Matrix Computation
9249.content:
The weighted sums for a fully connected neural-network layer can be calculated together. Put the preceding layer's activations in a vector and the connection weights in a matrix; their product produces a vector of weighted sums for the next layer's neurons. An [[Activation Function]] is then applied element by element.

This is the matrix view of [[Feedforward Neural Computation]]. It replaces many separately described neuron calculations with one structured operation, while preserving the same connections. Kelleher uses the view to explain why matrix-oriented hardware can accelerate repeated forward and training passes through a network.

9255.content: Real-number arithmetic is governed by closure, commutative and associative laws, distributivity, identities, and inverses. They supply the structural basis for [[Equivalent Equations]] and algebraic simplification.

9258.sourceSearchName: laws of exponents laws of exponents
9258.title: Laws of Exponents
9258.heading: Laws of Exponents
9258.content:
The laws of exponents summarize how repeated factors combine. For appropriate real values and integer exponents,

$$a^ma^n=a^{m+n},$$

$$\frac{a^m}{a^n}=a^{m-n}\quad(a\neq0),$$

$$(a^m)^n=a^{mn},$$

$$(ab)^n=a^nb^n.$$

Each law follows by counting and regrouping factors. The common-base requirement matters: exponents cannot be added merely because two powers are multiplied. These rules also explain the [[Zero Exponent]] and [[Negative Exponent]] conventions and support simplification of polynomial and rational terms.

9261.heading: Law of Sines
9261.content:
For a triangle with sides $a,b,c$ opposite angles $A,B,C$, the law of sines states

$$\frac{a}{\sin A}=\frac{b}{\sin B}=\frac{c}{\sin C}.$$

It solves triangles when an angle-side opposite pair is known. In the ambiguous side-side-angle case, the sine value may correspond to two supplementary angles.

9264.heading: Latitude and Longitude Graticules
9264.content: Latitude measures angular position north or south of the Equator, and its parallels form circles around Earth. Longitude measures angular position east or west of the prime meridian, and its meridians join the poles. One minute of latitude corresponds historically to one nautical mile, while the surface distance represented by a degree of longitude shrinks as the meridians converge poleward.

9267.title: Law of Formation
9267.heading: Law of Formation
9267.content:
A law of formation is a rule that generates the members of a pattern or [[Sequence]]. It can describe how to obtain each term from earlier terms or give a direct formula from the term's position.

For (2,7,12,17,\ldots), the recursive law adds five each time, while the direct law gives the (n)th term as (2+5(n-1)). A proposed law should reproduce every listed case and specify which positions are allowed. Algebraic notation makes the rule reusable without enumerating the infinitely many terms it can generate.

9270.heading: Law of Cosines
9270.content:
For a triangle with angle $C$ between sides $a$ and $b$, the law of cosines is

$$c^2=a^2+b^2-2ab\cos C.$$

It handles side-angle-side and side-side-side data. When $C$ is a right angle, $\cos C=0$, so the formula reduces to the [[Pythagorean Theorem]].

9276.title: Latent Variable
9276.heading: Latent Variable
9276.content:
A latent variable is included in a probabilistic description but is not directly observed in the available dataset or current question. It represents hidden structure that can explain dependencies, classes, states, or model choices among observed variables.

Inference assigns a distribution to the latent alternatives or marginalizes them. Learning with latent variables is an incomplete-data problem because parameter estimation must account for values that were not recorded.

9279.heading: Latent Semantic Representation
9279.content:
A latent semantic representation maps observed words and documents into hidden dimensions intended to capture recurring concepts or topics. Matrix factorization and probabilistic topic models reduce sparse vocabulary space by explaining co-occurrence through a smaller set of latent factors.

The representation can connect documents that discuss similar ideas with different words and reduce noise from synonymy or sparse counts. Its dimensions are learned from the corpus, so their stability and interpretation depend on the model, data, and chosen dimensionality.

A latent factor model represents users and items through a smaller set of learned dimensions that explain patterns in their interactions. The dimensions are not required to correspond directly to named attributes.

A preference score is produced from the relationship between a user's factors and an item's factors. This compact representation makes large sparse matrices more tractable while preserving the regularities most useful for prediction.

9285.title: Latency
9285.heading: Latency
9285.content:
Latency is the delay between an input event and the corresponding system response. In a tracked visual system, motion-to-photon latency covers the time from measuring the user's pose to displaying graphics from the resulting viewpoint.

Latency breaks the temporal agreement between bodily motion and external [[Feedback]]. It can reduce control performance, create registration errors in [[Augmented Reality]], and contribute to [[Cybersickness]]. Variability in the delay can also matter.

Sources include sensing, processing, simulation, rendering, and display refresh. Raising update rates, reducing scene complexity, or predicting motion may reduce parts of the delay, but improving only one stage does not remove every source.

For AR, latency is also a [[Temporal Registration|temporal-registration]] error: the physical view reflects the present while a virtual object is rendered from an older pose. Motion prediction can estimate the viewpoint expected at display time, but variable delay and sudden changes limit how well prediction can compensate.

In an online game, network latency delays the response to a remote player's command and may give faster connections a competitive advantage. Turn-based mechanics, regional or connection-quality matchmaking, prediction, and designs tolerant of timing variation can reduce its effect, but the acceptable delay depends on how precisely play must be synchronized.

9288.content:
Large margin nearest neighbor learning pulls designated same-class target neighbors together while penalizing different-class impostors that enter their neighborhoods. The learned Mahalanobis matrix is optimized for subsequent nearest-neighbor classification.

This combines a compactness objective with margin constraints around local neighborhoods. It is more targeted than maximizing global class separation because it concentrates on the pairs that can actually change a local prediction.

9291.title: Laplacian Score
9291.heading: Laplacian Score
9291.content:
Laplacian Score ranks a feature by its ability to keep nearby observations close after projection onto that feature. A graph represents local neighborhoods, and the graph Laplacian converts neighborhood preservation into a numerical score.

A low score indicates that the feature varies smoothly over the local data manifold. The method is label-free and efficient, but it evaluates features individually and can retain redundant attributes unless paired with an additional redundancy control.

9294.sourceSearchName: laplacian regularized metric learning laplacian regularized metric learning
9294.title: Laplacian Regularized Metric Learning
9294.heading: Laplacian Regularized Metric Learning
9294.content:
Laplacian regularized metric learning supplements labeled constraints with a graph built from labeled and unlabeled observations. A Laplacian penalty encourages nearby points on the data manifold to remain close after transformation.

The supervised term separates classes, while the graph term preserves local geometry inferred from abundant unlabeled data. Their relative weight controls whether labels or manifold structure dominates the learned distance.

9297.title: Laplacian Eigenmaps
9297.heading: Laplacian Eigenmaps
9297.content:
Laplacian Eigenmaps is a nonlinear dimension-reduction method that builds a neighborhood graph and embeds nearby observations close together in a lower-dimensional space. Eigenvectors of a graph Laplacian define the coordinates.

The method is designed to preserve local manifold structure rather than all pairwise distances. Its result depends strongly on how neighborhoods and edge weights are constructed.

9300.title: Landmark
9300.heading: Landmark
9300.content:
A landmark is an easily distinguishable object used to maintain spatial orientation, estimate distance or direction, and build landmark and route knowledge.

A global landmark is visible from much of the environment and supplies broad directional guidance. A local landmark supports decisions at a particular point. Effective landmarks are placed where they can be noticed and are visually distinct in color, texture, lighting, shape, or size.

Landmarks make environments more legible and support [[Wayfinding]], [[Spatial Knowledge]], and the construction of a [[Cognitive Map]].

An AR navigation system can highlight a physical landmark or attach a decision cue to it, connecting digital route information to a feature the traveler can recognize without the display. Stable real-world referents also help relate egocentric guidance to an exocentric overview.

9309.title: Laminar Flow
9309.heading: Laminar Flow
9309.content: Laminar flow occurs when fluid particles follow smooth, orderly streamlines that remain approximately parallel. Neighboring layers slide without large-scale mixing, so viscous effects dominate. It is favored by lower speed, smaller length scale, and greater kinematic viscosity; increasing the Reynolds number eventually destabilizes this organized regime.

Chart convergence is proportional to longitude change and the sine of the reference latitude, producing a constant convergence factor for the chart.

9315.heading: Laminar Flow Selection for Thermal Models
9315.content:
A laminar flow model assumes orderly viscous motion without resolving turbulent fluctuations. For internal pipe flow, Reynolds number compares inertia with viscosity and provides a regime check; the book's pipe examples keep the value below about 2,300.

Because density and viscosity may vary with temperature and pressure, a velocity that begins in the laminar range may not remain there throughout a heated system. 9321.heading: Lagrange Theorem
9321.content:
Lagrange's theorem states that the order of a subgroup of a finite group divides the order of the group. The quotient is the number of cosets, called the subgroup index.

It follows that element orders divide group order and that every group of prime order is cyclic.

9324.heading: Lagrange Multiplier Method
9324.content:
The Lagrange multiplier method finds candidate extrema subject to equality constraints by combining the objective and constraints in a Lagrangian. Stationarity requires the objective gradient to be a linear combination of constraint gradients.

The multipliers measure the local sensitivity of the optimum to constraint bounds. Candidate points still require feasibility and classification checks.

9327.title: Lagrange Interpolation
9327.heading: Lagrange Interpolation
9327.content:
Lagrange interpolation writes the interpolating polynomial as $p_n(x)=\sum_{i=0}^n L_i(x)f(x_i)$. Each [[Lagrange Basis Polynomial]] is one at its own node and zero at every other node.

The formula works for equally or unequally spaced points and gives a direct expression. Adding a new point generally requires rebuilding all basis polynomials.

9330.sourceSearchName: lagrange basis polynomial lagrange basis polynomial
9330.title: Lagrange Basis Polynomial
9330.heading: Lagrange Basis Polynomial
9330.content:
A Lagrange basis polynomial for node $x_i$ is $L_i(x)=\prod_{k\ne i}(x-x_k)/(x_i-x_k)$. It equals one at $x_i$ and zero at every other interpolation node.

These selector properties make the weighted sum in [[Lagrange Interpolation]] reproduce every supplied function value while remaining a polynomial of the required degree.

9336.title: Kubernetes
9336.heading: Kubernetes
9336.content:
Kubernetes is a container orchestrator that maintains and changes a declared set of container workloads. It creates instances, replaces failed ones, rolls out updated images, and routes work so the running system moves toward its desired configuration.

The book uses Kubernetes to operate replicated sales-order workers. Its value comes from orchestration rather than from changing the worker's business logic; the service must already be designed so multiple instances can safely share queued work.

9338.sourceSearchName: kubernetes self healing kubernetes self healing
9338.title: Kubernetes Self-Healing
9338.heading: Document

9339.sourceSearchName: kubernetes self healing kubernetes self healing
9339.title: Kubernetes Self-Healing
9339.heading: Kubernetes Self-Healing
9339.content:
Kubernetes self-healing is the controller behavior that replaces failed or removed workload instances to restore declared state. A pod is treated as disposable, while the deployment's desired replica count is treated as authoritative.

The book demonstrates this by deleting a worker pod and observing a replacement appear. Recovery keeps processing capacity available, but durable application state must live outside the replaceable pod.

9342.title: Kubernetes Replica
9342.heading: Kubernetes Replica
9342.content:
A Kubernetes replica is one desired copy of a pod managed by a workload controller. Increasing the replica count permits more instances of a scalable worker to run; reducing it removes excess instances.

The book changes the sales-order deployment from two replicas to three and reapplies the manifest. Replication improves throughput and availability only because queued work prevents every instance from processing the same input indiscriminately.

9345.title: Kubernetes Pod
9345.heading: Kubernetes Pod
9345.content:
A Kubernetes pod is the workload unit in which one or more closely related containers run. The sales-order deployment produces worker pods from the registered Docker image, and each pod can independently draw messages from the shared queue.

Pods are replaceable rather than durable identities. When one is deleted, the deployment controller creates another so the requested replica count is restored.

9348.title: Kubernetes Node
9348.heading: Kubernetes Node
9348.content:
A Kubernetes node is a machine in the cluster that supplies compute resources for pods. The orchestrator selects nodes when placing workloads and can distribute replicas across the available capacity.

Nodes are infrastructure beneath the application's pods, not copies of the application themselves. Managed Kubernetes reduces direct machine administration, but node count and size still shape capacity and cost.

9350.sourceSearchName: kubernetes load balancing kubernetes load balancing
9350.title: Kubernetes Load Balancing
9350.heading: Document

9351.sourceSearchName: kubernetes load balancing kubernetes load balancing
9351.title: Kubernetes Load Balancing
9351.heading: Kubernetes Load Balancing
9351.content:
Kubernetes load balancing distributes available work or traffic among replicated workload instances. In the order-processing example, the shared queue lets whichever worker is available claim the next message rather than binding work to a specific pod.

Adding replicas increases potential consumption capacity, while removing one leaves remaining workers able to continue. Effective balancing therefore depends on both the orchestrator and an application input mechanism designed for competing consumers.

9352.sourceSearchName: kubernetes load balancing kubernetes load balancing
9352.title: Kubernetes Load Balancing
9352.heading: References

9354.title: Kubernetes Deployment
9354.heading: Kubernetes Deployment
9354.content:
A Kubernetes deployment declares how an application workload should run, including its image, labels, container settings, and desired replicas. Applying the YAML definition asks the cluster to bring its current state into agreement with that declaration.

The sales-order deployment refers to the image stored in Azure Container Registry and exposes its replica count as configuration. Updating the file and applying it provides a repeatable scale or rollout operation.

9357.title: Krull Dimension
9357.heading: Krull Dimension
9357.content:
The Krull dimension of a ring is the supremum of the lengths of chains of distinct [[Prime Ideal]]s. It measures how many strict prime specializations the spectrum can contain.

The [[Prime Ideal Height]] measures chains below one prime, while a module's dimension is the dimension of the ring modulo its annihilator. The [[Hilbert-Samuel Polynomial]] gives another description of dimension in a Noetherian local setting.

9360.title: Kubernetes Cluster
9360.heading: Kubernetes Cluster
9360.content:
A Kubernetes cluster is the collection of compute and control resources on which containerized workloads are scheduled. It provides the environment in which nodes host pods and the control plane works to preserve declared deployments.

The AKS project creates a cluster as an Azure resource and connects command-line and dashboard tools to it. Cluster capacity and lifetime affect cost even when the application itself is idle.

9363.heading: Kruskal-Wallis Test
9363.content:
The Kruskal–Wallis test compares a continuous or ordinal response across three or more independent groups using ranks. It is a nonparametric alternative to [[One-Way ANOVA]] when parametric assumptions are not credible.

The omnibus statistic can establish that the group distributions are not all alike, but it does not identify the differing pairs. As with other rank tests, interpretation is clearest when the shapes of the group distributions are also examined.

9366.sourceSearchName: krull intersection theorem krull intersection theorem
9366.title: Krull Intersection Theorem
9366.heading: Krull Intersection Theorem
9366.content:
For an ideal I in a Noetherian ring and a finitely generated module M, the intersection of all IⁿM is annihilated by an element 1−a with a ∈ I. If I lies in the [[Jacobson Radical]], this intersection is zero.

The theorem shows that repeated multiplication by a sufficiently small ideal eventually separates every nonzero module element. Its proof uses the [[Artin-Rees Lemma]].

9369.title: Koszul Homology
9369.heading: Koszul Homology
9369.content:
Koszul homology is the homology of a [[Koszul Complex]] after its differential is defined by a sequence of ring elements. It measures the failure of that sequence to behave regularly.

For a regular sequence on a ring, every positive-degree Koszul homology module is zero and H₀ is the quotient by the sequence. Patterns of vanishing can be used to extract regular subsequences.

9372.title: Koszul Complex
9372.heading: Koszul Complex
9372.content:
The Koszul complex of elements r₁,…,rₙ is a finite complex whose terms are exterior powers of a free module and whose differential contracts with the chosen sequence.

It encodes algebraic dependence among the elements. If they form a [[Regular Sequence]], positive [[Koszul Homology]] vanishes and degree-zero homology is the quotient by their generated ideal.

9414.heading: Kleene Star
9414.content:
The Kleene star of a language S is S* = S⁰ ∪ S¹ ∪ S² ∪ …, the set of strings formed by concatenating zero or more strings from S. Because S⁰ = {ε}, every Kleene closure contains the [[Empty String]].

When Σ is treated as a set of one-symbol strings, Σ* is exactly the set of all finite [[String|strings]] over the [[Alphabet]] Σ. The same operator supplies repetition in a [[Regular Expression]].

9441.heading: Kernel Trick for Classification
9441.content:
The kernel trick replaces an inner product between explicit feature vectors with a kernel function equal to an inner product in an implicit transformed space. A linear separator in that space can represent a nonlinear boundary in the original variables.

This avoids constructing every transformed coordinate, but prediction must evaluate the kernel against support vectors. Kernel choice and its parameters determine the geometry in which margin maximization occurs.

9444.title: Kernel of Ring Homomorphism
9444.heading: Kernel of Ring Homomorphism
9444.content:
The kernel of a ring homomorphism consists of source elements mapped to zero. It is an ideal because it is closed under subtraction and multiplication by arbitrary source elements.

The homomorphism is injective exactly when its kernel is the zero ideal.

9447.title: Kelley-Salisbury Method
9447.heading: Kelley-Salisbury Method
9447.content:
The Kelley-Salisbury method iteratively estimates standardized multiple-regression weights from a predictor correlation matrix and a vector of predictor-criterion correlations. It adjusts the coefficient associated with the largest residual validity until the trial validities converge.

The procedure is systematic and easy to program. In the book's treatment, it can obtain a solution even when predictors are statistically dependent.

The homomorphism is injective exactly when its kernel contains only the source identity.

9453.title: Keep It Simple Principle
9453.heading: Keep It Simple Principle
9453.content: Keep It Simple Stupid (KISS) treats unnecessary complexity as a design risk. A solution should contain enough structure to meet the present requirement, but avoid extra layers, conditions, or abstractions that make its behavior harder to understand and maintain. Simplicity does not mean ignoring essential error handling or future change; it means keeping each chosen mechanism proportional to the problem it actually solves.

9456.title: KDD Process
9456.heading: KDD Process
9456.content:
The KDD process begins by understanding the application and end-user goals, then selects a target data set, cleans and preprocesses it, reduces or projects its representation, chooses a method and algorithm, performs mining, interprets the patterns, and incorporates the knowledge.

Loops among these stages are expected. A poor pattern may reveal the need for different data, attributes, parameters, or even a revised question.

9459.title: Karush-Kuhn-Tucker Conditions
9459.heading: Karush-Kuhn-Tucker Conditions
9459.content:
The Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions extend [[Lagrange Multiplier Method|Lagrange multiplier reasoning]] to inequality constraints. They combine primal feasibility, multiplier sign restrictions, stationarity, and complementary slackness.

Complementary slackness connects each multiplier to its constraint: an inactive inequality has zero multiplier, while a positive multiplier can occur only for an active constraint. Under convexity conditions, the conditions can also be sufficient for optimality.

9462.title: Karma
9462.heading: Karma
9462.content:
Karma is a JavaScript test runner that starts a web server, launches a browser, executes source code against configured tests, and reports results. It supplies the runtime environment in which Jasmine-defined Angular tests operate.

The runner can watch source changes and execute the suite again, giving quick feedback while a component or service is developed.

9465.title: Kaplan-Meier Estimator
9465.heading: Kaplan-Meier Estimator
9465.content:
The Kaplan–Meier estimator calculates survival as the product of conditional event-free proportions at observed event times. It is nonparametric because it does not assume a particular distribution for event times.

The estimator incorporates right-censored observations through the changing risk set. Stratified Kaplan–Meier curves provide descriptive group comparisons, while tests or regression are needed for formal inference and confounder adjustment.

9468.title: Kanban
9468.heading: Kanban
9468.content:
Kanban is a method for visualizing, measuring, and managing the flow of work. A [[Kanban Board]] makes states and queues visible, while limits on [[Work in Progress]] expose constraints and encourage finishing before starting more.

Unlike Scrum, Kanban does not require a Sprint timebox or replace existing roles. It is especially useful for production and support work that arrives continuously or follows a recurring flow.

9471.title: Kanban Board
9471.heading: Kanban Board
9471.content:
A Kanban board maps work items across columns that represent workflow states. Cards and queues reveal where work is active, waiting, blocked, or completed, allowing a team to inspect the entire flow at a glance.

The board should reflect the real process rather than an idealized one. Dates, buffers, and work limits can be added when they help measure [[Cycle Time]] or expose a [[Bottleneck]].
